anatomy.lede: Built on the same plan as a garden woodlouse, the giant isopod is an armoured box of segments and legs, enormously scaled up.

hotspots.label: Antenna
hotspots.text: Every isopod has two pairs of antennae, along with compound eyes and four sets of jaws.

hotspots.label: Head shield
hotspots.text: The two triangular compound eyes sit at the front of the head, about 25 mm apart.

hotspots.label: Mouthparts
hotspots.text: Fish, squid and crabs were the most common foods found in the guts of giant isopods caught off Yucatán, Mexico.

hotspots.label: Walking legs
hotspots.text: Each of the seven segments of the thorax carries its own pair of walking legs.

hotspots.label: Body segments
hotspots.text: Overlapping armoured plates cover the seven thorax segments; behind them, the short abdomen has segments of which one or more fuse into a tail.

senses.lede: The giant isopod has large eyes in a world with almost no light, and they are badly damaged by sunlight.

senses.name: Light-gathering eyes
senses.text: Each eye is about 18 mm along its top edge and holds roughly 3,500 facets. Cells packed with tiny clear vesicles behind the light-sensitive parts are thought to reflect light back through them.

senses.name: Forward-facing view
senses.text: The eyes face forwards and slightly down, and their fields of view may overlap a good deal.

senses.name: Blinded by daylight
senses.text: Isopods brought up from the deep and exposed to daylight suffered severe damage to their light-sensitive cells, which did not recover even after two months in darkness.

body.lede: Beneath the armour, the giant isopod breathes and swims with the same limbs.

systems.title: Gills that paddle
systems.text: Under the abdomen, branched limbs called pleopods do two jobs: they exchange gases like gills and beat to swim. Giant isopods are seldom seen swimming, though one has been filmed coming in to land.

systems.title: Large eggs, not more eggs
systems.text: Although far bigger than other isopods, a female carries about the same number of eggs. Instead, egg size seems to grow almost in step with body size.

systems.title: Ordinary on the inside
systems.text: The male reproductive organs look much like those of smaller isopod species.

survival.lede: A slow scavenger on the dark seafloor, the giant isopod eats what falls from above and whatever cannot get away.

tactics.title: Scavenging
tactics.text: Gut contents support the idea that it is mainly a scavenger of dead animals, especially fish, squid and crustaceans.

tactics.title: Easy prey
tactics.text: It also feeds on fixed or slow-moving animals, such as echinoderms and sea squirts.

life.lede: Giant isopods skip the larval stage entirely: the young leave their mother's pouch looking like small adults.

stages.name: Brooded egg
stages.text: Females lay eggs into a brood pouch, the marsupium, on the underside of the body and carry them until the young are ready to emerge.

stages.name: Manca
stages.text: The young, called mancae, look like miniature adults but lack the seventh pair of legs.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Isopods trapped off Yucatán, at 349–733 m, ranged from 4.4 to 36.5 cm long.

stages.name: Breeding
stages.text: Far more males and females were mature in February than in August, suggesting that reproduction is seasonal.
